messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ali, a 22-year-old Middle Eastern man, had been working as an auditor in downtown Chicago for just over a year when he was brutally raped one night after leaving his office. The smell of stale cigarettes and the taste of alcohol still triggered vivid flashbacks to that traumatic event, which left him feeling constantly on edge. Since then, Ali found himself hypervigilant around any reminders of the incident. The scent of cigarette smoke during a late-night meeting at a client’s office would send his heart racing, and he often felt the urge to flee the room immediately. This experience had led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies: he made sure to stay close to exits in unfamiliar places, wore concealing clothing to avoid drawing attention to himself, and avoided situations where others might evaluate his appearance or performance. The moral violation he experienced during the assault also heightened his sensitivity to people misbehaving. During a recent audit at a local business, Ali found it impossible to concentrate as he was reminded of his rapist’s behavior. He felt an overwhelming urge to leave, which only intensified when someone mentioned his ex-partner in conversation. The reference made him feel even more vulnerable and triggered intense feelings of humiliation. Ali’s negative appraisals exacerbated these reactions. He often thought that somebody else would not have ended up in the same situation as he had, deepening his sense of self-blame and loss of happiness. These thoughts were reinforced by his avoidance behaviors; every time he avoided an evaluation or stayed close to a door, it seemed to validate his belief that something terrible could happen again. The constant threat perception fueled Ali’s maladaptive strategies further. He became extremely wary of sudden movements from others, often freezing in place if someone approached quickly. His body felt perpetually tense and ready to react to danger, which made even everyday tasks feel exhausting. The sense of being constantly threatened by his environment reinforced his habit of avoiding unfamiliar places and people who might trigger memories. Ali’s colleagues noticed that he was less engaged at work, often choosing to sit in corners or near exits during meetings. He had grown increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and events where he feared encountering similar triggers. This withdrawal led to fewer opportunities for feedback and collaboration, impacting his professional growth. His fear of being evaluated made him hesitant to take on new projects that might expose him to further scrutiny. The self-reinforcing cycle tightened as Ali’s negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies grew stronger over time. The more he avoided certain situations and reminders, the more entrenched his belief became that danger lurked around every corner. His body remained perpetually tense, amplifying each trigger into a full-blown reaction of fear and anxiety. Ali finally sought help when he realized that his work performance was slipping and he felt increasingly isolated from his peers. He feared that if things continued this way, he would lose not only his job but also any chance at a fulfilling life. Despite the overwhelming sense of humiliation and constant threat, Ali hoped that therapy could provide some relief and help him regain control over his life. In summary, Ali’s experience was marked by a cycle of triggers leading to heightened anxiety, which in turn reinforced his maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals. The traumatic event had left deep scars on both his professional and personal life, making it increasingly difficult for him to function without constant fear and avoidance.
